Within the ESS infrastructure project speciﬁcally, work composition skews toward mandated security compliance work including continuous vulnerability remediation (ACAS-driven), STIG compliance, and POA&M tracking. These compliance categories represent a substantial share of ESS work. In aggregate across the portfolio, approximately 90 percent of tickets carry priority equivalent to Sev 3 or Sev 4; the remaining 10 percent carry Sev 1 or Sev 2. Current-state constraints relevant to forward-looking scoping include a single-host deployment in which compute, scheduling, and the database run on one Linux host; manual rather than scheduled refresh of the Zephyr test-management data; and a derived- views and analytics layer that is still maturing. The capability handles data from Military Health System sources, including clinically relevant defect and support records. Source connectivity uses DoD public key infrastructure certiﬁcate trust and token-based authentication, with credentials managed outside the codebase. The software is maintained under a software-assurance posture aligned to NIST SP 800-218, including software bill-of-materials generation, software composition analysis, and static analysis. 28 5. In-ﬂight Initiatives The ESS environment is subject to a number of in-ﬂight modernization and transition initiatives that affect the supported infrastructure, applications, and tooling during and beyond the recompete window. The active storage migration to the vSAN-based platform is described in Section 2.9 (Hardware Lifecycle Posture). A migration of source code repositories from Subversion to GitLab is active. Container adoption through Docker is expanding in scope and footprint. The

The average TI.com compute utilization is 15.3% (total compute available is ~2,600,000 MHz) and the average TI.mil compute utilization is 12.4% (total compute available is ~1,250,000 MHz). TI.com average storage utilization is 38.2% (total storage available is ~470 TiB) and TI.mil average storage utilization is 18.7% (total storage available is ~425 TiB). The equipment used to provision resource pools (i.e., servers and networking and storage devices) is owned by DHMS. A complete hardware inventory for both the METIC and the DDC is provided as an attachment, enumerating manufacturer, asset description, sub- type, quantity, and location for each item. Lifecycle posture is described in Section 2.9. The ESS environment supports approximately 2,400 virtual machines across two virtualization environments, designated TI.com and TI.mil. The TI.com environment hosts approximately 70 percent of the total VM count; TI.mil hosts the remainder. A third VDI- speciﬁc vCenter exists but is currently offline. 8 The two environments share a converged physical infrastructure rather than running on physically separated host pools. Individual hypervisor hosts within the TI.com environment routinely serve workloads from both the TI.com and TI.mil VM populations, and s

vironment routinely serve workloads from both the TI.com and TI.mil VM populations, and shared networks carry traffic from both. Workload separation between the two environments is logical rather than physical. Recent utilization metrics indicate that approximately one-third of the total VM inventory is powered off but retained. Of the active, powered-on VMs, a portion operate at near-zero CPU utilization, resulting in approximately half of the aggregate VM inventory showing minimal active operational use. Additionally, current utilization data indicates that some active VMs are conﬁgured with capacity exceeding their actual workload requirements, while storage capacity is occupied by long-retained snapshots and thin-provisioning overhead. The current VM inventory spans two governance layers. Core ESS infrastructure VMs are managed under the ESS infrastructure project's authority. Program-supported VMs, including but not limited to those associated with DHMSM, JOMIS, EIDS, and FEHRM- managed workloads, are managed under their respective program's authority and require program engagement for any disposition. To complete the analysis, the Defense Healthcare Management Systems (DHMS) engineering leaders visited the testing site to understand the physical layout and how the testers use the devices and equipment, reviewed technical diagrams, studied test use cases, and gathered inventories of the equipment used across the ESS environment. Based on the above research, the services and capabilities have been divided into six sections: • Section 1: The physical environment itself, the Medical Enterprise Test Innovation Center (METIC) 1 is the physical testing location designed for employees and vendors (either virtually or in person) to manage and run tests to support DHMS health care technology. The scope of this includes the physical location, furnishings, electricity, heating and cooling, management of physical equipment, and physical testing layout. • Section 2: The computer infrastructure includes network connectivity and conﬁguration, compute resources, storage, speciﬁc medical devices used for testing, laptops, mobile devices and security services. • Section 3: Testing has three sections. The ﬁrst describes the Developmental Test and Evaluation (DT&E) services in scope. The second provides illustrations of use cases that describe how the testing is comp

cooling, and electrical wiring to properly support the equipment. The remaining 52% accommodates nine offices, a kitchen, two conference rooms (20 person and 8 person) and touchdown workspaces for up to 30 support personnel. The large conference room includes audio-visual capability and videoconferencing for meetings and whiteboards used for technical discussions. A small percentage of the space hosts a reception area with a badge-only door behind it that is used to access the facility. The average number of people using the facility for testing is 30 per day, while at peak test events, the number can increase to 75 testers per day onsite. In total, there are 184 active users of the TI.com environment and 308 active users of the TI.mil environment (includes development vendors) who can participate on site or through remote connections. Procurement is coordinated by the PEO DHMS Asset Lifecycle Management team, with the partner providing operational support throughout the lifecycle from requirement identiﬁcation through procurement and disposition. PEO DHMS provides funding to DHA for procurement execution. The operational workﬂow proceeds as follows: the partner identiﬁes a need (typically driven by approaching end-of-life of an asset, license renewal date, or capacity demand); the partner and the PEO ALM team conduct back-and-forth validation to conﬁrm need, right-sizing, and technical speciﬁcations; the PEO ALM team submits the validated procurement action to DHA; and DHA executes the procurement with PEO DHMS funding. Coordination between the partner and the PEO ALM lead occurs through recurring meetings held one to two times per month, supplemented by ad-hoc coordination on speciﬁc procurement actions as they arise. Any seed damaged or lost, while in the custody of the Contractor, will be replaced (if available) by the Government, and actual cost to the Government for replacement will be deducted from payments due the Contractor. All unused seed shall be returned to the pickup point by the Contractor or nearer destination, if so directed, upon completion of work or termination of the contract. D. Seeding Operation 1. Rate of Seeding - Seed shall be distributed at the rate stated in the Detailed Specifications, or as directed by the Contracting Officer. Some seeding rates may be slightly reduced due to availability of seed. 2. Seeding Conditions - Seed shall not be applied when the wind speed exceeds ten miles per hour unless permission is given by the COR in writing. It may also be desired by the Government that the ground be covered by a minimum of two inches of snow during seeding operations. Therefore, seeding may be delayed if there is no snow on the ground and snow is expected in the weather forecast. 3. Coverage - The entire surface within the designated boundaries of the job area shall receive uniform coverage with the seed except for such areas as may be excluded by Government. Areas excluded from seeding operations within the wor

overed. Contractor cannot apply seed if seeding equipment will disturb project area in any way. Any wheel, track, or other marks will not be allowed. 7. Tests for uniformity and rate of application - The Government will make tests as operations progress to determine uniformity of seeding. Standards of performance will be determined by adequate monitoring on each individual path and for each seeding strip covered. All monitoring will be done by the Government at no cost to the Contractor. Should the Contractor wish to object in any way to the monitoring done at any particular time by the Government, the Contractor shall be present in person or by authorized representative to voice said objections when said monitoring samplings are done, and to agree upon new records and/or samples at the time, where after the monitoring sampling done by the Government shall be final and binding in the settlement of the contract. E. Work Stoppages - The Government reserves the right to stop seeding operations at any time when seeding conditions are considered sufficiently unfavorable to warrant stoppage. Stoppage shall continue until seeding operations are again authorized by the Government. Because of the nature of the work, any time for which work is suspended by the Government becaus

Award may not necessarily be made to the Offeror(s) submitting the lowest price. Award may not be made on all items depending on availability of funds and seed.
